entry: Stalk-like posterior part of the brain, connecting the [[Cerebrum|cerebrum]] with the [[Spinal cord|spinal cord]]. In the human brain it comprises the midbrain, the pons and the medulla oblongata, and sometimes the diencephalon. It makes up only around 2.6 percent of the brain's total weight, yet it regulates heart and [[Breathing|breathing]] rates and the body's [[Sleep|sleep]] cycle. It provides the main motor and sensory nerve supply to the face and neck through ten pairs of cranial nerves. It also carries motor and sensory pathways between the brain and the body, including the corticospinal tract for motor function and the spinothalamic tract for [[Pain|pain]], temperature, itch and crude touch. Dysfunction of the substantia nigra, a midbrain group of [[Dopamine|dopamine]]-using neurons, is implicated in [[Parkinson's disease]].

Irish writer, [[Barrister|barrister]] and theater manager, author of the Gothic horror novel *Dracula* (1897). He created the fictional character [[Count Dracula]]. He spent ten years in the civil service at Dublin Castle, during which he was also a drama critic. He was personal assistant and business manager to the actor Henry Irving at the West End's Lyceum Theater, which Irving owned. The novel is regarded as a milestone of Gothic and [[Vampire|vampire]] literature, and Stoker has been called "the father of vampire fiction."

Major groups into which the sciences are divided: formal, natural and social. The formal sciences, such as [[Logic|logic]] and [[Mathematics|mathematics]], study abstract structures described by formal systems, using *a priori* rather than empirical methods. The [[Natural science|natural sciences]] study natural phenomena and divide into physical and life sciences. The [[Social science|social sciences]] study human behavior in its social and cultural aspects. Applied fields such as [[Engineering|engineering]] and [[Medicine|medicine]] draw on them.

Name, term, design, symbol or other feature that distinguishes one seller's goods or services from those of others. Branding in the original sense of marking by burning is thought to have begun with [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egyptians]], who branded livestock and, as early as 2,700 BCE, slaves. The word comes from the Old Norse *brandr*, meaning to burn. The term later extended to packaging and goods such as [[Oil|oil]], [[Wine|wine]] and [[Cosmetics|cosmetics]], and in the 21st century to services, political parties and people's stage names. In [[Marketing|marketing]] and [[Business|business]], brand equity is the measurable totality of a brand's worth, and brand valuation assigns it a monetary value.

Collection of six instrumental works by [[Johann Sebastian Bach]] (BWV 1046–1051). Bach presented them in 1721 to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, under the French title *Six Concerts avec plusieurs instruments* (Six Concertos for several instruments), though they were probably composed earlier. Some pieces feature several solo instruments in combination, and the scoring draws on a wide range of [[Orchestra|orchestral]] instruments. The first movement of Concerto No. 1 is based on an introduction to Bach's 1713 cantata *Was mir behagt*, and Concerto No. 5 features a prominent [[Harpsichord|harpsichord]] part. The concertos are widely regarded as some of the greatest orchestral compositions of the Baroque era.

Spirit produced by distilling [[Wine|wine]], generally containing 35–60% alcohol by volume. It is typically drunk as an after-dinner digestif. Some brandies are aged in wooden casks, while others are colored with caramel to imitate aging. Cognac and Armagnac from [[France|southwestern France]] are among the most renowned. The term also covers pomace brandy and other fruit brandies, which are called eau de vie. In the early 16th century French brandy helped start the cross-Atlantic triangle trade, until cheaper [[Rum|rum]] replaced it as the trade's alcohol in the late 17th century.

Planned federal capital of [[Brazil]] and the Federal District. Founded by President Juscelino Kubitschek on April 21, 1960, to replace [[Rio de Janeiro]] as the national capital, it was planned in 1956 by Lúcio Costa, Joaquim Cardozo and [[Oscar Niemeyer]], who also designed its white modern buildings. The city is laid out in the shape of an airplane, and it was inscribed as a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] in 1987 for its [[Modern architecture|modernist architecture]] and [[Urban planning|urban planning]]. Brasília is Brazil's third-most populous city, with 2.8 million people. All three branches of the federal government are located there, and it hosts 124 foreign embassies.

[[Alloy]] of [[Copper|copper]] and [[Zinc|zinc]], in proportions that can be varied to achieve different colors and properties. Brass is similar to [[Bronze|bronze]], which uses tin instead of zinc. Its relatively low melting point (900 to 940 °C; 1,650 to 1,720 °F, depending on composition) and high workability make it easy to cast and machine. It is used for locks, hinges, gears, bearings, zippers, [[Plumbing|plumbing]] and [[Valve|valves]], where [[Corrosion|corrosion]] resistance and low friction are needed, and for horns and bells in [[Musical instrument|musical instruments]]. It is unsuitable for marine use because salt water leaches the zinc, but marine brass containing tin avoids this. The density of brass is 8.4 to 8.73 g/cm³, and almost 90% of brass alloys are recycled.

Class of [[Musical instrument|musical instruments]] that produce sound by sympathetic vibration of air in a tubular resonator, driven by the player's lips. Slides, valves, crooks or keys change the length of tubing, and the player's embouchure, lip tension and air flow select the harmonic produced. Classification follows how sound is made, not the material: wooden instruments such as the alphorn and didgeridoo are brass instruments, while the [[Saxophone|saxophone]] is a [[Woodwind instrument|woodwind]] made of brass. Valved instruments include the [[Trumpet|trumpet]], horn, euphonium and [[Tuba|tuba]], while the [[Trombone|trombone]] is a slide instrument. Natural instruments, such as the bugle, play only notes of the harmonic series and are used for period performances.

Economically important family of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] known as the mustards, crucifers or cabbage family. Most species are herbaceous, with simple leaves that lack stipules. Flowers have four free sepals, four free petals and six stamens. The family includes cruciferous vegetables such as [[Cabbage|cabbage]], [[Broccoli|broccoli]], [[Cauliflower|cauliflower]], kale, turnip, [[Radish|radish]] and [[Horseradish|horseradish]], as well as [[Rapeseed|rapeseed]] and the model organism *Arabidopsis thaliana*. Butterflies of the family Pieridae, such as *Pieris rapae*, are among the best-known pests of commercial crops. As of 2023 the family was divided into two subfamilies, and as of September 2025 it contained over 350 accepted genera. Garlic mustard, an extremely [[Invasive species|invasive]] species in the United States, can be toxic to butterfly larvae.

Capital and largest city of [[Slovakia]], the fourth largest city on the [[Danube]]. It lies on both banks of the river at the foot of the Little Carpathians, on the border of [[Austria]] and [[Hungary]], and is the only national capital with land borders with two other sovereign states. [[Vienna]] lies just 50 km (31 mi) away, making the two the closest pair of capitals in Europe. The city proper has about 479,000 people, and the metropolitan area about 1.3 million. Bratislava was the coronation site and legislative center of the [[Kingdom of Hungary]] from 1536 to 1783, when eleven Hungarian kings and eight queens were crowned in St Martin's Cathedral. Today it is the seat of the Slovak president, parliament and government, and of the Supreme Court. It is the 19th-richest region of the [[European Union]] by GDP (PPP) per capita.

Dystopian novel by [[Aldous Huxley]], written in 1931 and published in 1932. Set in a World State where citizens are engineered into an intelligence-based social hierarchy, it anticipates advances in reproductive technology, sleep-learning and psychological conditioning. Its [[Utopia|utopian]] society is challenged by an outsider, John the Savage. Huxley later wrote the essay *Brave New World Revisited* (1958) and the utopian novel *Island* (1962). The title comes from [[William Shakespeare]]'s *The Tempest*, where the phrase is used ironically. The novel is often paired with [[George Orwell]]'s *Nineteen Eighty-Four* (1949). It ranked fifth on the Modern Library's list of the 100 Best Novels in English of the 20th century in 1998 and 1999, and it has been frequently banned and challenged.

Men's [[Association football|association football]] team representing [[Brazil]], nicknamed Canarinho. Administered by the Brazilian Football Confederation, it has been a [[FIFA]] member since 1923. Brazil has won the [[FIFA World Cup|World Cup]] five times (1958, 1962, 1970, 1994 and 2002), more than any other national team. Many commentators regard its 1970 side as the greatest football team of all time. Its most notable rivalries are with [[Argentina]], Italy and Uruguay.

Edible seed of *Bertholletia excelsa*, a large South American tree. It is one of the largest and longest-lived trees in the [[Amazon rainforest]], reaching 50 m (160 ft) tall and possibly living 500 years or more. The fruit weighs as much as 2 kg (4.4 lb) and holds eight to 24 wedge-shaped seeds. Brazil nuts are notable for micronutrients, especially a high amount of [[Selenium|selenium]]. The trees fruit almost exclusively in pristine forests, because [[Pollination|pollination]] requires large bees that disturbed forests lack. Agoutis, large rodents, gnaw open the fruit and bury seeds, some of which germinate. In 2024 world production was 79,736 tonnes, with [[Brazil]] and [[Bolivia]] accounting for 87%. The wood is prized for carpentry, flooring and heavy construction.

Extensive region covering most of eastern, southern and central [[Brazil]]. It covers some 4,500,000 km² (1,930,511 sq mi), approximately half of the country's land area. The vast majority of Brazil's population (203,062,512 in the 2022 census) lives in the highlands or on the narrow coastal region beside them. Ancient [[Basalt|basaltic]] lava flows formed much of the region, which has no seismic or volcanic activity today. [[Erosion]] has shaped it into sedimentary deposits and worn-down mountains. Its diversity includes several [[Biome|biomes]], varied climates, many [[Soil|soil]] types and thousands of animal and plant species. The highlands are usually divided into the Atlantic Plateau along the eastern coast, the Southern Plateau and the Central Plateau, where about 85% of the land was once covered by [[Cerrado]] vegetation. The highest point is Pico da Bandeira, 2,891 m (9,485 ft), in the Serra do Caparaó.

[[Martial arts|Martial art]] and combat sport based on grappling, ground fighting and submission holds, commonly abbreviated as BJJ. Practitioners take an opponent to the ground, gain a dominant position and use joint locks, chokeholds or compression locks to force submission. It rests on the idea that a smaller, weaker person can defeat a larger opponent through leverage and weight distribution. Brothers Carlos, Oswaldo, Gastão Jr. and Hélio Gracie developed it around 1925, after Carlos was taught [[Judo|judo]] in 1917 by Mitsuyo Maeda or one of his students. Training includes sparring, called rolling, and can be done with a gi or without one. It is considered essential for modern [[Mixed martial arts|mixed martial arts]].

Capital and largest city of the [[Republic of the Congo]], on the north bank of the [[Congo River]]. It lies directly opposite [[Kinshasa]], capital of the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]], and the two are the only national capitals in the world on opposite banks of a river within sight of each other. Its population is estimated to exceed 2.1 million, more than a third of the national total. The Italian-French explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza officially founded the settlement on September 10, 1880, on the existing Bateke settlement of Ncuna. Within the [[French colonial empire|French colonial]] system it served as the de facto capital of Free France from 1940 to 1942, during [[World War II]]. In 2013 [[UNESCO]] designated it a City of Music.

Edible fruit-bearing tree in the [[Moraceae|mulberry and jackfruit family]], *Artocarpus altilis*. Its name refers to the texture of the moderately ripe fruit when cooked, similar to freshly baked bread. The fruit is a staple in many cultures, and the light, sturdy timber is used for furniture, houses and surfboards. Austronesian expansion spread the tree into [[Oceania]], where it is believed to have been selectively bred in [[Polynesia]] from the breadnut. British and French navigators introduced seedless Polynesian varieties to the Caribbean in the late 18th century. A single tree can produce up to 200 or more grapefruit-sized fruits per season, and it grows to 26 m (85 ft) tall. Most selectively bred [[Cultivar|cultivars]] are seedless, and large-scale propagation uses root cuttings. The tree is closely related to the [[Jackfruit|jackfruit]].

Processed food made from [[Cereal|cereal]] grains, eaten mainly in the morning or as a snack, primarily in Western societies. Warm cooked cereals such as [[Oat|oatmeal]] have the longest history, but ready-to-eat cold cereals, many made by extrusion, appeared in the late 19th century. Ferdinand Schumacher, a German immigrant, began the cereal revolution in 1854 with a hand oats grinder in Akron, Ohio, and his German Mills American Oatmeal Company was the nation's first commercial oatmeal manufacturer. The number of types of breakfast cereal in the United States more than doubled, from about 160 in 1970 to around 340 in 1998. Many packaged cereals have a high [[Sugar|sugar]] content and are marketed to children with cartoon [[Mascot|mascots]] and toys. The industry has gross profit margins of 40–45%.

First meal of the day, usually eaten in the morning. The English word refers to breaking the fasting period of the previous night, and by around the 15th century it was used in written English for a morning meal. In [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]], peasants ate soup, beer, bread and onions before work, and a traditional breakfast was fūl, made from fava beans, with emmer-wheat bread and [[Falafel|falafel]]. The Romans called the meal ientaculum, typically bread, cheese, olives and cold meat. In [[Middle Ages|medieval]] Europe breakfast was eaten mainly by working people, children, the elderly and the sick, when only two formal meals a day were eaten. Customs now vary: French breakfasts tend to be light, with [[Bread|bread]], butter, jam and [[Coffee|coffee]], while the full English breakfast includes eggs, [[Bacon|bacon]], [[Sausage|sausages]], grilled tomatoes, mushrooms, baked beans and toast.

American neo-Western crime drama television series created by [[Vince Gilligan]] for AMC. Set in [[Albuquerque, New Mexico|Albuquerque]], it follows high school chemistry teacher Walter White, played by [[Bryan Cranston]], who begins making [[Methamphetamine|methamphetamine]] after a diagnosis of stage-three [[Lung cancer|lung cancer]] to secure his family's finances. The series ran for five seasons and 62 episodes, from January 20, 2008, to September 29, 2013. Critics widely regard it as one of the greatest television series, and it won 16 Primetime Emmy Awards. It spawned the spin-off *Better Call Saul* and the film *El Camino: A Breaking Bad Movie*.

Ending of an intimate relationship, romantic or platonic. Slang calls a breakup started by one partner "dumping." For a married couple the ending is typically called a separation or [[Divorce|divorce]]. Psychotherapist Susie Orbach (1992) has argued that the end of dating and cohabiting relationships can be as painful as divorce, because such relationships are less socially recognized. Platonic breakups are usually caused by failure to maintain a [[Friendship|friendship]]. In 1976 sociologist Diane Vaughan proposed an "uncoupling theory," in which one partner unconsciously knows the relationship is ending but may hold on for years. Breakups act as acute stressors, often producing [[Insomnia|insomnia]] and [[Depression (mood)|depression]].

Disintegration of the [[Yugoslavia|Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia]] in 1991–92. After economic and political crisis in the 1980s, its constituent republics split apart. Between June 1991 and April 1992, four republics declared independence while [[Serbia]] and [[Montenegro]] remained federated. [[Germany]] took the initiative in recognizing [[Croatia]] and [[Slovenia]]. Unresolved ethnic tensions led to the [[Yugoslav Wars]] from 1991 to 2001, most severe in Croatia and [[Bosnia and Herzegovina]]. A new constitution adopted on April 27, 1992, formally ended the breakup and established the rump Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

Cancer of the mammary glands, most commonly arising in cells lining the milk ducts or lobules. Risk factors include [[Obesity|obesity]], lack of exercise, [[Alcohol (drug)|alcohol]] consumption, hormone replacement therapy during [[Menopause|menopause]], [[Ionizing radiation|ionizing radiation]], older age and family history. About five to ten percent of cases result from inherited predisposition, including BRCA mutations. Diagnosis is confirmed by [[Biopsy|biopsy]]. Five-year survival rates are over 90% in the United States and the United Kingdom but lower in developing countries. Treatment may include surgery, [[Radiation therapy|radiation therapy]], [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]], hormonal therapy and targeted therapy. Worldwide it is the leading type of cancer in women, accounting for 25% of all cases; in 2018 it caused two million new cases and 627,000 deaths.

Either of two prominences on the upper front of the torso in humans and other [[Primate|primates]]. Both sexes develop breasts from the same embryonic tissues, and their size is a major secondary sex distinction. In females the breasts contain [[Mammal|mammary]] glands that produce and secrete milk to feed infants. Female humans are the only mammals that permanently develop breasts at [[Puberty|puberty]], driven by [[Estrogen|estrogens]] together with growth hormone. The [[Nipple|nipples]] can be an erogenous zone, and breasts can represent fertility, femininity or abundance. Some cultures regard bare breasts in public as indecent, and breasts have been featured in sculpture, art and photography.
